headline: How Steve Jobs Showed the First iPhone on Stage

sentences.text: Steve Jobs showed a new phone in January 2007.
The test phone did not work very well.
He followed a clear order of quick steps.
He used the phone to find a coffee store.
He called and ordered four thousand drinks for fun.

grammar.title: Simple Past Tense
grammar.note: The simple past tense is used to express an action that was completed at a specific time in the past. Here, 'showed' describes what Steve Jobs did during the 2007 presentation.

grammar.title: Infinitive of Purpose
grammar.note: An infinitive phrase (to + base verb) can function as an adverbial modifier explaining why an action was performed. Here, it gives the reason why he used the phone.

sentences.text: In January 2007, Steve Jobs showed a new phone to people.
The early test model barely worked because it was not ready.
So Jobs followed a very strict order of steps on stage.
He opened Google Maps and found a local coffee shop nearby.
He called the shop and ordered four thousand lattes for fun.
Then he said it was a wrong number and hung up.

grammar.title: Adverb Modifying a Verb
grammar.note: The word 'barely' is a negative adverb meaning 'hardly' or 'only just.' It modifies 'worked' to emphasize that the prototype was close to failing.

grammar.title: Omission of That in Reporting
grammar.note: In informal and spoken English, the conjunction 'that' is frequently dropped after reporting verbs like 'said.' The clause 'it was a wrong number' acts directly as the direct object of 'said.'

sentences.text: When Steve Jobs introduced the first iPhone in January 2007, it was fragile.
The prototype, which is an early test version, could easily break down.
Jobs had to follow a strict sequence of steps during his presentation.
During the live demonstration, he used Google Maps to locate a nearby Starbucks.
He called the store directly from the stage and jokingly ordered 4,000 lattes.
Jobs quickly told the clerk that he had dialed the wrong number.

grammar.focus: which is an early test version
grammar.title: Non-defining Relative Clause
grammar.note: Relative clauses starting with 'which' and enclosed in commas give optional, extra details about a noun. Here, it defines what 'The prototype' means without changing the main sentence message.

grammar.title: Past Perfect Tense
grammar.note: The past perfect tense (had + past participle) indicates an action that occurred prior to another past event. Dialing the number happened before Jobs told the clerk about the mistake.

sentences.text: When the original iPhone was introduced by Steve Jobs in 2007, it was far from complete.
The prototype, an early experimental model, was notoriously unstable and prone to crashing during use.
To prevent embarrassing technical glitches on stage, a precise sequence of actions was rehearsed.
Every feature had to be shown in a specific order so the device would stay functional.
During the presentation, Jobs used Google Maps to search for a local Starbucks store nearby.
He placed a live phone call to the coffee shop in front of the audience.
Jobs playfully ordered 4,000 lattes to go before stating that he had called the wrong number.

grammar.title: Passive Voice
grammar.note: The passive voice (be + past participle) places primary emphasis on the receiver of the action rather than the doer. Here, 'the original iPhone' takes subject position instead of Steve Jobs.

grammar.focus: so the device would stay functional
grammar.title: Adverbial Clause of Purpose
grammar.note: The conjunction 'so' introduces a clause expressing purpose or target result. It explains why the presentation steps had to be followed in a rigid sequence.

sentences.text: When Steve Jobs unveiled the original iPhone in January 2007, the revolutionary device was still a fragile work in progress.
Behind the polished presentation, the early prototypes—experimental test units—were exceptionally bug-ridden and prone to sudden system crashes.
To ensure the live demonstration proceeded smoothly, engineers devised a meticulously choreographed sequence of actions that Jobs followed.
Deviating even slightly from this carefully scripted path could have caused the unreleased smartphone to freeze completely.
At one memorable moment during the keynote presentation, Jobs launched Google Maps to find a nearby Starbucks store.
He dialed the location directly from the stage, seamlessly demonstrating the device's integrated calling and mapping features.
When a clerk answered, Jobs playfully requested 4,000 lattes to go before quipping that he had called the wrong number.
The legendary prank delighted the crowd while cleverly masking the nerve-wracking technical precariousness behind Apple's historic product launch.

grammar.title: Modal Perfect for Unfulfilled Past
grammar.note: The modal perfect structure 'could have + past participle' expresses a past possibility that was avoided. It highlights the high technical risk involved during the live keynote.

grammar.title: Participle Clause for Simultaneous Action
grammar.note: A present participle phrase (-ing) attached to a main clause describes an action occurring concurrently with the main verb. Here, it shows what Jobs was demonstrating while dialing.
